reasoning: Failure-driven edits (Group 1) are all kept: the number-matching replacement, the CATEGORY CHECK, the quoted-title-anchor and definition-style rule, the altered-title and English-name rules, the part-of-entity-in-clue rule, and the final checklist. Group 2's definition-style/headword bullet covered the same point as Group 1's definition-style bullet. I kept the failure version and folded in the one non-redundant detail, which is to copy the dictionary headword exactly. The other Group 2 edits cover patterns the failure edits do not address, so I kept them: reverse team-name case, noisy-context rare-word anchoring, title-character-of-film, word-count hint, code expansion, set-phrase headwords, media cues, and part-of-name clues. None of these conflict with the failure edits. For example, 'Last name of...' -> 'Michelin' is compatible with 'Chester' -> 'Arthur'. Every insert uses a distinct target, so ordering does not conflict, and nothing touches the protected markers.

edits.target: - Use the singular form for a generic single object ('Well', not 'wells'), but keep the plural for crops, commodities and mass categories ('Bananas') or when the clue says 'these'/'ones'.
edits.content: - Number: match the clue's grammatical subject. If the clue's subject or described items are plural ('the canvas-covered blades of a windmill' -> 'Sails'; 'these ...'; 'ones'), give a countable answer in the plural form. Use the singular only when the clue describes one single item ('one of these', 'this <object>') -> 'Well', not 'wells'. Keep the plural for crops, fruits, commodities and mass categories ('Bananas'; 'Coupes A L'Ananas are desserts made with this tropical fruit' -> 'Pineapples').

edits.target: - Ask: what category is the answer (country, person, vitamin, object, band), and what member of that category fits all the clue details?
edits.content: - CATEGORY CHECK (do this before answering any 'this <noun>' clue): write down the noun after 'this/these' ('country', 'nation', 'site', 'part of the tree'). The answer must itself be an instance of that noun. Reject any candidate that (a) is a name or word already in the clue, (b) is a component, product or feature that the clue says is IN, ON or PART OF the answer, or (c) is a process or abstract term when the noun asks for a thing. The answer is usually the CONTAINER or WHOLE that the clue describes. 'Many of this country's finest red wines come from the Coonawarra region' -> 'Australia' (not 'Coonawarra'). 'A 15 1/2-mile causeway connects this Persian Gulf nation to the Saudi mainland' -> 'Bahrain' (not the causeway's name). 'One of the buildings at this British site is named for Robert Devereux, held there before his execution' -> 'Tower of London' (not 'Devereux Tower'). 'Water is lost to the atmosphere through this part of the tree' -> 'Leaves' (a part; 'transpiration' is the process). Repeated passage phrases such as 'King Fahd Causeway' or 'Devereux Tower' only show which facts the clue is built on; they are not the answer.

edits.target: - Honor qualifiers when the context offers several names for the same thing: 'Greek god of erotic love' -> 'Eros' (not Roman 'Cupid').
edits.content:
- A clue that is only a descriptor plus a quoted title ('A 1961 classic: "West Side Story"', 'A 1990 film: "Pretty Woman"') uses the title as an ANCHOR. The answer is NOT the quoted title. It is the related work or person the passages link to it with words like 'adaptation of', 'based on', 'inspired by', 'retelling of', 'written by'. 'West Side Story' -> 'Romeo and Juliet', because the passages say 'a modern-day retelling of Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet'. Scan the passages for that link phrase and answer with the thing it points to. Never answer with the title already in the clue.
- Definition-style clues with no 'this' ('An Anglican parish priest', 'Term for the circle that encloses a comic strip character's dialogue', 'It's the part of a racetrack from the last turn to the finish line'): answer with the single standard term that the passages gloss with the clue's own words ('parish priest ... usually called a vicar or rector' -> 'Vicar'). Dictionary and glossary passages repeat the definition almost verbatim, and their titles or first words give the headword ('Homestretch - definition of homestretch ...'); copy the headword exactly as it appears there. Do not pick a related but different rank or role ('Curate' is an assistant, not the parish priest). Give the bare generic head word without a modifier that the passages add ('balloon', not 'speech balloon'). When several synonyms appear, choose the one named first or most often beside the clue's key words.

edits.target: - For titles, give the standard title without quotation marks and keep internal punctuation as written in the context ('M*A*S*H', not 'MASH film').
edits.content:
- Altered or parody titles: when the clue says a spoof, episode or short 'changed X to Y in this <work/title>' ('changed "All" to "Oil" in this Shakespeare title'), the answer is the ORIGINAL work ('All's Well That Ends Well'), not the altered title that the passages mention ('Oil's Well That Ends Well'). Undo the substitution the clue describes and give the full original title.
- English form of names: when the clue is in English and uses an English type noun ('this Florentine palace', 'this cathedral', 'this bridge'), answer with the English-language name ('Pitti Palace', not 'Palazzo Pitti'; 'Tower of London'), even if many passage titles use the native form. A leading 'the' is optional.

edits.target: - Put only the bare answer in the answer tags. Do not write a sentence, restate the clue, or add dates, qualifiers or alternatives. Brief reasoning belongs before the tags.
edits.content: - Part of the entity already in the clue: if the clue gives part of a name or title ('the only U.S. President named Chester', 'this man, first name John'), answer only the REMAINING part as an answer key would ('Arthur', not 'Chester A. Arthur'). If the clue gives a role or descriptor noun ('this manicurist in Palmolive ads', 'this president'), answer with the bare name ('Madge', not 'Madge the Manicurist'). If the clue contains a foreign-language or untranslated word ('Coupes A L'Ananas ... this tropical fruit'), the answer is the English common name for it ('Pineapples'), never the foreign word.

## Final check before writing <answer> (run every time)
1. Strike from the answer every word the clue already states, including first names, role nouns ('manicurist', 'president', 'fruit') and foreign-language forms of a clue word. A word may stay only when it is the head noun of a proper name, per the Rule 4 exception.
2. If a passage repeats the clue verbatim with an archived answer, the answer must be that archived form. Do not extend it with a descriptor taken from other passages.
3. Check the number: plural clue subject -> plural answer.
4. The answer must not equal the title, name or term quoted or named in the clue. It must be the thing the clue points to.
5. Category check: the answer must be an instance of the noun after 'this/these' (country, site, part, person), and be the whole or container the clue describes, not a component, causeway, building, region or process mentioned inside the clue.

edits.target: Other named entities in the clue are anchors, never the answer.
edits.content: - Reverse case: when the clue names a player, coach or game and asks for 'this team' ('this team's Phil Simms'), the player is the anchor. Answer with the full team name as the passages repeat it, city included ('New York Giants'), not just the city or a bare nickname.

edits.target: - Otherwise, build the answer from passages that match several of the clue's details.
edits.content: - In very noisy contexts, most passages are only keyword hits on one common word (e.g. film titles containing 'Sweetheart'). Look for the single passage that combines the clue's rarest words (e.g. 'mannequins' + 'sweetheart' + 1920s) and take the answer from it. Treat an epithet in the clue ('sweetheart of an actress') as a hint to the nickname phrase the passage uses ('America's sweetheart'). Answer with the person or thing it names (Mary Pickford), not the epithet.

edits.target: 'One of these <role/title>' ('the 14th one of these spiritual leaders') asks for the title or category noun itself (Dalai Lama), not the individual named in the clue.
edits.content: - 'The title character of this film / play / book' (clue: 'Poet Pablo Neruda befriends the title character of this recent film set in Italy') asks for the WORK's title ('Il Postino'). Do not answer with the character's personal name or with the person already named in the clue. Drop quotation marks around the title.

edits.target: If a bare number appears in parentheses, treat it only as this hint, not as part of the question.
edits.content: - A word-count hint inside the clue ('this 3-word actors' phrase', 'this two-word term') is a hard filter, like the letter count: the answer must have exactly that many words, so reject shorter or longer candidates ('Break a leg' fits, 'Break' does not).

edits.target: and answer with the common English name (Conch).
edits.content:
- A clue that ends in a short all-caps code or abbreviation after a slogan or phrase ('Let freedom ring: PHL') asks you to expand the code (airport code, state or country abbreviation, ticker) into the full place or entity name ('Philadelphia'). Use the slogan or phrase only to confirm which expansion fits. Give the bare name, with no state or country added.
- 'This phrase / term / expression / saying' clues want the complete set phrase as a dictionary or encyclopedia headword, with every word and its internal hyphens ('Hit-and-run', 'Break a leg'). Do not shorten it to one word, and do not add the noun the clue already supplies ('accident', 'driver', 'actors').
- Media cues in the clue ('heard here', 'seen here', 'shown here', 'pictured') refer to an audio or video clue you cannot perceive. They are decoration. Archive copies of the clue keep these words, so match the remaining textual hooks ('wandering minstrel', 'handheld percussion instrument') against the passages and copy the archived answer ('tambourine').

edits.target: Still apply the person-name rule above.
edits.content: - Part-of-name clues ('Last name of the French brothers who...', 'First name of...', 'Initials of...', 'Surname of...'): give ONLY the requested part ('Michelin'), never the full name, the family or group label ('Michelin brothers'), or a single member's full name ('Andre Michelin').
